newsitem.title: USA: No consensus yet on US commodity law revisions.
newsitem.headline: No consensus yet on US commodity law revisions.

text.p: There is no consensus yet on how to update the Commodity Exchange Act, the basic law governing the U.S. futures industry, a high-ranking Senate Agriculture Committee staff worker said Wednesday.
Although the issue appears moribund, discussions were proceeding behind the scenes and progress was being made, said Randy Green, chief of staff for the committee.
"We don't yet (have consensus). But I believe progess is being made to that end," Green said at a conference sponsored by American Agri-Women.

Most contoversial among the potential revisions were proposals to clarify the boundaries of the 1972 Treasury amendment and to create "professionals only" markets for institutions and deep-pocket investors.
Green said those two ideas were "equally controversial."

Committee chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, remains optimistic that consensus will be reached, he said. Lugar would prefer to obtain general agreement on a bill before scheduling a "mark-up" session for his committee. Lugar had hoped to hold a mark-up before Memorial Day.

Green declined to suggest when a bill-drafting session would be called. He told reporters that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and other regulatory agencies were involved in the ongoing discussions in search of consensus.
